title: Reverse a Linked List
description: Given the head of a singly linked list, reverse the list and return its new head. A linked list node is represented as an object with `val` and `next` properties.

starterCode.python:
def reverse_list(head):
    # Write Python code here
    prev = None
    curr = head
    while curr:
        next_temp = curr.next
        curr.next = prev
        prev = curr
        curr = next_temp
    return prev

hint: Use three pointers: prev, curr, and nextTemp to reverse links as you traverse.
approach: To reverse a linked list, we iterate through the list and change each node's next pointer to point to its predecessor. We need to save the next node before overwriting the pointer so we don't lose the remaining nodes.

title: Check Balanced Parentheses
description: Given a string `s` containing just the characters '(', ')', '{', '}', '[' and ']', determine if the input string is valid. The brackets must close in correct order.
hint: Push opening brackets onto a stack. When you see a closing bracket, pop from the stack and check if it matches.
approach: We use a Stack. When encountering an opening bracket, push it. For a closing bracket, pop the top of the stack and ensure they match. If the stack is empty at the end, the string is balanced.

title: Find Duplicates in Array
description: Given an integer array `nums`, return `true` if any value appears at least twice in the array, and return `false` if every element is distinct.
hint: You can use a Hash Set to store visited numbers and check if the current number has already been seen in O(N) time.
solution:
const set = new Set(nums);
return set.size !== nums.length;
approach: Use a HashSet to keep track of numbers we have already seen. If we add a number that is already in the set, we immediately return true. Otherwise, return false after checking all.

title: BFS Traversal
description: Perform a Breadth-First Search traversal on an adjacency list graph starting from node `start` and return the array of traversed nodes in order.
hint: Use a Queue and a visited Set. Enqueue the starting node. While the queue is not empty, dequeue a node, record it, and enqueue all its unvisited neighbors.
approach: BFS uses a Queue to visit nodes level-by-level. Starting from the source, we explore all immediate neighbors first, tracking visited nodes in a set to prevent infinite cycles.

title: Binary Search Implementation
description: Write a function `binarySearch(arr, target)` that takes a sorted array `arr` and a `target` number, and returns the index of the target. Return `-1` if it is not found.
hint: Keep left and right pointers. Find the middle element. Shrink the search range by comparing the middle element to the target.
approach: Binary Search halves the search space at each step. By checking the element at index mid = (left + right) / 2, we decide whether to search left or right, running in logarithmic time.

title: Stack using Queue
description: Implement a Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) stack using only standard queue operations. Implement push, pop, and top.
hint: When you push an element, rotate the queue so that the newly added element becomes the front of the queue.
solution: push(x) { this.q.push(x); for(let i=0; i<this.q.length-1; i++) this.q.push(this.q.shift()); }
approach: To make a queue behave like a stack, when pushing a new element, we enqueue it, and then shift all other elements behind it, placing the newest element at the front.

title: Detect Cycle in Linked List
description: Given the head of a linked list, check if the list has a cycle. Return `true` if there is a cycle, and `false` otherwise.
hint: Use Floyd's Cycle-Finding Algorithm: two pointers moving at different speeds (fast and slow). If they meet, there is a cycle.
approach: Floyd's Tortoise and Hare algorithm uses two pointers. The fast pointer moves twice as fast as the slow one. If there is a cycle, the fast pointer will eventually loop and catch up to the slow one.

title: Merge Sorted Arrays
description: Given two sorted integer arrays `arr1` and `arr2`, merge them into a single sorted array. Keep linear O(N + M) complexity.
hint: Use two pointers, one for each array. Compare elements and push the smaller one to the output array.
approach: With two pointers, we compare the current element of both sorted arrays. We append the smaller value and advance its pointer, merging the remaining values at the end.

title: Find Height of Binary Tree
description: Given the root of a binary tree, find its maximum height (depth). An empty tree has height 0.
hint: The maximum depth of a binary tree is 1 + the max depth of its left and right subtrees. Solve recursively.
solution:
if (!root) return 0;
return 1 + Math.max(maxDepth(root.left), maxDepth(root.right));
approach: The depth of a tree is calculated recursively. For any node, the height is 1 plus the maximum height of its left and right children. Base case is a null node returning 0.

title: Count Islands in Grid
description: Given a 2D grid of 1s (land) and 0s (water), count the number of islands. An island is surrounded by water and is formed by connecting adjacent lands vertically or horizontally.
hint: Traverse the grid. When you hit a '1', trigger DFS or BFS to sink the entire island (turn connected 1s into 0s) and increment your island count.
approach: We perform a scan of the 2D grid. Whenever we find land ('1'), we start a depth-first search that recursively visits all neighboring land tiles, marking them as water ('0') to prevent recounting. Each initial land tile found represents one island.

title: Longest Common Subsequence
description: Given two strings `text1` and `text2`, return the length of their longest common subsequence. A subsequence of a string is a new string generated from the original string with some characters deleted without changing relative order.
hint: Use a 2D DP table. If characters match: dp[i][j] = 1 + dp[i-1][j-1]. If not: dp[i][j] = max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]).
approach: LCS is solved using Dynamic Programming. We create a grid to compare character match states. If characters at indices match, we extend the subsequence length from the diagonal value. Otherwise, we carry over the maximum from the top or left cells.

title: 0/1 Knapsack Problem
description: Given weights `wt` and values `val` of `n` items, and a knapsack capacity `W`, find the maximum value you can put in the knapsack. Each item can either be taken or left (0/1).
hint: Use a DP array of size W + 1. For each item, update the array from right to left: dp[w] = max(dp[w], dp[w - wt[i]] + val[i]).
approach: This is the classic 0/1 Knapsack problem. Using dynamic programming, we track the maximum value achievable for all weight capacities from 0 up to W. Running iterations backwards helps us reuse a 1D state array without double-counting items.

title: Dijkstra Shortest Path
description: Implement Dijkstra's shortest path algorithm. Given a weighted graph represented as an adjacency list and a starting node, return an object containing the shortest distances from start node to all other nodes.
hint: Initialize distances of all nodes as infinity and start node as 0. Repeatedly pick the unvisited node with minimum distance and update its neighbors' distances.
approach: Dijkstra's algorithm finds the shortest path in a weighted graph. We maintain a distance list initialized to Infinity. At each step, we pick the closest unvisited node, freeze its distance, and update neighbors by checking if routing through this node decreases their cumulative path cost.

title: Validate BST
description: Given the root of a binary tree, determine if it is a valid binary search tree (BST). A node's left child value must be strictly smaller, and right child strictly larger.
hint: Use recursion. Pass minimum and maximum allowable bounds down the tree: `validate(node, min, max)`. If node value violates bounds, return false.
approach: To validate a BST, it's not enough to check left < node < right for adjacent nodes. The left subtree must be entirely less than the node, and the right entirely greater. We propagate min/max boundary constraints recursively down the tree.

title: Coin Change Problem
description: You are given an integer array `coins` representing coins of different denominations and an integer `amount`. Return the fewest number of coins that you need to make up that amount. Return `-1` if impossible.
hint: Create a DP array of size amount + 1 filled with Infinity, except dp[0] = 0. For each coin, loop from coin value to amount: dp[i] = min(dp[i], dp[i - coin] + 1).
approach: Using Dynamic Programming, we compute the minimum number of coins needed for every value up to the target amount. For each currency denomination, we check if adding one coin to an already solved subproblem decreases the coin count.

title: Word Break Problem
description: Given a string `s` and a dictionary of strings `wordDict`, return `true` if `s` can be segmented into a space-separated sequence of one or more dictionary words.
hint: Use DP. Let dp[i] be true if s[0...i-1] can be segmented. Update dp[i] by checking if there is a j < i such that dp[j] is true and s[j...i-1] is in dictionary.
approach: Word break determines if a sentence is buildable from words. We use a boolean DP array where dp[i] means text up to index i is segmentable. We scan backward for matching suffix words in the dictionary.

title: Merge Intervals
description: Given an array of intervals where `intervals[i] = [start_i, end_i]`, merge all overlapping intervals, and return an array of the non-overlapping intervals.
hint: Sort the intervals by their start time. Iterate through, merging the current interval with the last merged interval if they overlap.
approach: We sort intervals chronologically by start value. We push the first interval to a list. For subsequent entries, we check for overlaps. If overlapping, we stretch the boundary. Otherwise, we add it as a new interval.

title: Maximum Subarray (Kadane)
description: Given an integer array `nums`, find the contiguous subarray (containing at least one number) which has the largest sum and return its sum.
hint: Use Kadane's Algorithm. Iterate through the array. Keep track of current sum. Reset current sum to 0 if it goes below 0. Max sum is maximum current sum seen.
approach: Kadane's algorithm evaluates contiguous subarrays. At each element, we decide whether to add it to our existing running sum, or throw away the historical sum and start fresh from the current index.

title: Serialize/Deserialize Binary Tree
description: Design an algorithm to serialize a binary tree into a string and deserialize that string back into a binary tree. The serialization format is up to you (e.g. comma-separated values).
hint: Use pre-order traversal. For serialization, represent null nodes with a specific character like 'N'. For deserialization, use a queue to reconstruct node children recursively.
solution: serialize(root); deserialize(data);
approach: Tree serialization encodes 3D hierarchy into a flat string. We use pre-order traversal (Node-Left-Right) and mark empty leaf edges with 'N' to ensure the exact structure is reconstructible during parsing.

title: Top K Frequent Elements
description: Given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`, return the `k` most frequent elements. You may return the answer in any order.
hint: Build a frequency map. Sort the keys of the map based on frequency values, and return the top k keys.
approach: We aggregate item occurrences into a key-frequency hashmap. We then sort the keys by frequency in descending order and extract the top k items.

title: KNN Classifier
description: Implement a simplified 1-Nearest Neighbor classifier. Given an array of training coordinates `trainX` (each an array of numbers), their labels `trainY` (array of integers), and a single query point `queryX`, find the label of the closest training point using Euclidean distance.
hint: For each point in trainX, calculate its Euclidean distance to queryX. Find the index of the minimum distance, and return the label at that index in trainY.
approach: KNN measures geometric distance. For a query point, we loop through all training samples, compute Euclidean distances, and return the category label of the sample with the smallest distance.

title: Calculate Metrics
description: Given the counts of True Positives (`tp`), False Positives (`fp`), False Negatives (`fn`), and True Negatives (`tn`), return an array containing `[accuracy, precision, recall, f1]` rounded to 2 decimal places.
hint: Accuracy = (tp + tn) / total. Precision = tp / (tp + fp). Recall = tp / (tp + fn). F1 = 2 * (p * r) / (p + r). Handle division by zero carefully.
approach: Evaluation metrics measure classifier quality. Accuracy checks total correct. Precision checks correctness of positive predictions. Recall checks fraction of positive cases found. F1 is their harmonic mean.

title: Gradient Descent Step
description: Perform a single weight update step for a parameter `w` in gradient descent. Given current weight `w`, learning rate `lr`, and derivative of loss with respect to weight `dw`, return the updated weight rounded to 4 decimal places.
hint: The formula is: w_new = w - lr * dw. Use `.toFixed(4)` to round correctly.
solution: return +(w - lr * dw).toFixed(4);
approach: Gradient descent moves parameters opposite the slope gradient. By subtracting learning rate times the derivative (dw) from weight (w), we slide toward the error minimum.

title: Euclidean Distance
description: Write a function `euclideanDistance(p1, p2)` that returns the Euclidean distance between two multi-dimensional coordinate arrays of equal length. Round to 2 decimal places.
hint: Calculate sum of squared differences for each dimension: `(p1[i] - p2[i]) ** 2`. Take square root of sum.
approach: Euclidean distance computes straight-line distance in multi-dimensional space by taking the square root of the sum of squared coordinate differences.

title: Normalize a Dataset
description: Implement Min-Max normalization. Given an array of numbers `data`, rescale each value to fit between `0` and `1` using Min-Max scaling. Round values to 2 decimal places.
hint: Min-Max formula is: x_scaled = (x - min) / (max - min). If max === min, default scaled values to 0.5.
approach: MinMax scaling bounds features between 0 and 1. We find the min and max values, then map each element x relative to the scale range.

title: Find Best K (Inertia)
description: In K-Means, the 'elbow method' finds the optimal cluster count. Given an array of `inertia` values from K=1 to K=N, return the index K (1-based) where the 'elbow' (steepest decrease drop changes) is located.
hint: Calculate differences between consecutive inertia values. The elbow is the point where the rate of drop slows down most dramatically.
approach: The elbow method identifies the optimal cluster number. We locate the elbow by finding the vertex where the drop rate between consecutive steps drops off most rapidly.

title: Linear Regression Predict
description: Write a function `predict(X, w, b)` that takes an array of input values `X`, a slope weight `w`, and a bias y-intercept `b`, and returns an array of predicted outputs where $y = w \times x + b$.
hint: Use map or loop through the input array X and evaluate y = w * x + b for each element.
solution: return X.map(x => w * x + b);
approach: Linear regression predicts continuous results. The prediction line is defined by y = wx + b. We apply this linear transform to each coordinate in feature vector X.

title: Confusion Matrix
description: Build a binary confusion matrix from predicted and actual labels. Given arrays of `actual` labels (0s and 1s) and `predicted` labels, return an object `{tp, fp, fn, tn}` representing True Positives, False Positives, False Negatives, and True Negatives.
hint: Iterate through both arrays. If actual===1 and predicted===1, increment tp. If actual===0 and predicted===1, increment fp, and so on.
approach: A confusion matrix reports classification counts. True Positives: actual 1, predicted 1. False Positives: actual 0, predicted 1. False Negatives: actual 1, predicted 0. True Negatives: actual 0, predicted 0.

title: Calculate Entropy
description: In decision trees, entropy measures impurity. Given the counts of two classes in a split node `c1` and `c2`, calculate the Shannon Entropy: $H(S) = -p_1 \log_2(p_1) - p_2 \log_2(p_2)$. Return the entropy rounded to 2 decimal places. Return 0 if the node is pure.
hint: Total = c1 + c2. p1 = c1 / total, p2 = c2 / total. Entropy = -p1 * log2(p1) - p2 * log2(p2). Log2 can be calculated as Math.log(p) / Math.log(2).
approach: Entropy evaluates partition impurity. In a binary split, we find the class fractions p1 and p2. We sum their log base 2 values scaled by their proportions. Pure splits yield 0 entropy.

title: Sigmoid Activation
description: Implement the sigmoid activation function: $S(x) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-x}}$. Write a function `sigmoid(x)` that returns the squeezed value rounded to 4 decimal places.
hint: The mathematical formula is: 1 / (1 + Math.exp(-x)). Wrap the return value with `.toFixed(4)` and convert to number.
solution: return +(1 / (1 + Math.exp(-x))).toFixed(4);
approach: The sigmoid function squashes any real-valued number into a probability range between 0 and 1. It acts as an activation threshold mapping in logistic neural nets.
